feedback.pattern: Pointer-replacement logic in two-child removal case
feedback.explanation: This test regressed and then recovered through three distinct code changes to the remove logic. The first change (run 50) consolidated the insert check and remove call into a single `root = removeHelper(root, i, b)` statement, which correctly propagates the new root back up the tree. However, runs 53–54 show a critical regression: the successor-selection logic was inverted—the code was searching the left subtree for the in-order successor instead of the right subtree, and was incorrectly linking `bottom.left = cur.left` before establishing the successor's right child. This caused the tree structure to collapse, producing inverted size values (expected 4 but got 14). The fix at run 55 corrected the successor search to traverse right while exploring viable candidates, properly maintained the predecessor pointer, and ensured correct pointer reassignment. The test passed after run 55 because the remove method correctly handled all three deletion cases: leaf nodes return NULL_NODE, single-child nodes return the non-null child, and two-child nodes properly splice in the in-order successor while preserving both subtrees.
nextSteps: Review the three cases of BST removal in isolation: (1) leaf deletion returns NULL_NODE to detach the node, (2) single-child deletion returns the child to bypass the node, (3) two-child deletion finds the in-order successor (smallest element in the right subtree), splices it into the removed node's position, and returns the modified subtree. The key insight is that each case returns a node reference that replaces the current node in its parent—this pointer-replacement pattern is essential for maintaining tree structure without explicit parent pointers.

When implementing two-child removal, trace through a concrete example (e.g., removing a node with both children) to verify that the successor's left subtree is correctly attached and the successor's right child is properly set. The successor is always greater than the left subtree and less than the right subtree, so its placement must preserve BST ordering.

This pattern recurs in EditorTrees Milestone 3 (delete with AVL rebalancing) and Exam 2 (pruneFullSubtreesSize3); both use the same pointer-replacement technique to detach or restructure subtrees, so mastering the return-value propagation here will transfer directly.

feedback.pattern: Iterative in-order traversal state management with flag-based node revisiting
feedback.explanation: This test failed across runs 26–39 before passing at run 40. The early runs (26–30) produced NullPointerException on Stack.push, assertion errors on value comparisons, and null returns. The fix at run 40 involved a substantial refactor of the next() method: the code introduced a two-flag system to track node visitation state (flag 1 for first visit, flag 2 for return visit after processing children). The change added logic to pop the current frame, check if it has a right child, and conditionally re-push the node with flag 2 only if the right child exists and the current node is not the one being returned. This prevents duplicate returns and ensures the stack correctly interleaves left subtree, current node, and right subtree in in-order sequence. The test passed after run 40 because the iterator correctly yielded nodes in sorted order by managing the traversal state through explicit flags.
nextSteps: Understand iterative in-order traversal as a state machine: each node must be visited three times (before left, between left and right, after right), and a flag or counter tracks which phase you are in. When you pop a node with flag 1, push it back with flag 2 and process the left child; when you pop it with flag 2, return its value and process the right child. This explicit state management is the core of stack-based traversal.

When implementing next(), be careful about the order of operations: pop the frame, check the flag, decide whether to return the value or push children. The condition `if (bottom != cur.left)` in the code indicates a check to avoid re-pushing a node that is already being processed—trace through a small tree to see why this matters.

This pattern recurs in EditorTrees toString() (which must run in O(N) via in-order traversal) and Exam 3 (which verifies mirror trees by comparing traversal outputs); mastering the flag-based state machine here will make those implementations clearer.

feedback.pattern: Two-child removal successor selection and pointer reassignment
feedback.explanation: This test failed across runs 45–54 before passing at run 55. The early failures (runs 45–51) produced size 2 when size 3 was expected, indicating that a subtree was being lost during removal. The root cause was inverted successor-selection logic: the code was searching the left subtree instead of the right, and was not correctly maintaining the successor's children. The fix at run 55 corrected the successor search to traverse right while comparing values, introduced explicit predecessor tracking, and ensured that the successor's left child is set to the removed node's left subtree and the successor's right child is set to the removed node's right subtree. This preserves both subtrees and maintains the BST property. The test passed after run 55 because the advanced removal case (removing a node with two children from a larger tree) correctly spliced in the in-order successor without losing any nodes.
nextSteps: For two-child removal, the in-order successor is the smallest element in the right subtree. Find it by going right once, then left as far as possible. Once found, the successor must be spliced into the removed node's position: its left pointer becomes the removed node's left subtree, and its right pointer becomes the removed node's right subtree (or the remainder of the right subtree if the successor was not the direct right child). Trace this on a tree where the successor is deep in the right subtree to see why predecessor tracking is necessary.

Verify that your successor-selection loop terminates correctly and that you handle the case where the successor is the direct right child (no left subtree) separately from the case where it has a left subtree. The pointer reassignments must happen in the correct order to avoid losing references.

This pattern recurs in EditorTrees Milestone 3 (delete with rebalancing) and Exam 2 (pruneFullSubtreesSize3); both require the same successor-selection and pointer-replacement logic, so understanding the mechanics here will transfer directly.

feedback.pattern: Breadth-first or exhaustive search implementation for non-BST containment
feedback.explanation: This test failed across runs 1–8 before passing at run 9. The early runs show a compilation error (containsNonBST method missing), followed by runs 3–8 with incorrect logic that returned false when the element was present. The fix at run 9 added a complete implementation of containsNonBST (20 lines) that uses a queue-based breadth-first search to visit every node in the tree, regardless of BST ordering. This approach exhaustively searches all nodes without relying on left/right comparisons to prune the search space. The test passed after run 9 because the method correctly identified whether the target element exists anywhere in the tree.
nextSteps: Understand the difference between contains (which exploits BST ordering to search in O(log n) time by going left or right based on comparison) and containsNonBST (which must search all nodes in O(n) time because the tree may not be a valid BST). containsNonBST requires a full traversal—either breadth-first with a queue or depth-first with a stack or recursion—visiting every node until the target is found or all nodes are exhausted.

When implementing exhaustive search, use a queue (for BFS) or stack (for DFS) to manage the frontier of unvisited nodes. For each node, check if it matches the target; if not, add its children to the frontier. This pattern is fundamental to graph and tree traversal and will appear in many future problems.

This pattern recurs in Exam 2 (shortestWordAlongPath navigates via BST ordering but accumulates state along the path) and EditorTrees get(int pos) (which uses rank instead of key comparison); understanding when to exploit structure (BST ordering) versus when to search exhaustively (non-BST trees) is a key algorithmic skill.

feedback.pattern: Iterative pre-order traversal stack initialization and node ordering
feedback.explanation: This test failed across runs 19–24 before passing at run 25. The early runs produced assertion errors on boolean checks and null pointer exceptions. The fix at run 25 involved a substantial refactor: the code added proper version tracking for concurrent modification detection, ensured the root is pushed to the stack only if it is not NULL_NODE, and captured the version at iterator construction time. The change also corrected the stack initialization and push order: children are pushed in reverse order (right first, then left) so that left is popped first, ensuring pre-order traversal visits the current node first, then the left subtree, then the right subtree. The test passed after run 25 because the iterator correctly yielded nodes in pre-order sequence by managing the stack initialization and push order correctly.
nextSteps: Understand pre-order traversal as visiting the current node before its children: the sequence is root, left subtree, right subtree. In an iterative stack-based implementation, push children in reverse order (right first, then left) so that the left child is popped and processed before the right. This is the opposite of in-order, where you must revisit nodes with flags.

When initializing the iterator, check that the root is not NULL_NODE before pushing it to the stack. Also capture the tree's version (or size) at construction time to detect concurrent modifications if the tree is modified during iteration—this is a defensive programming practice that prevents subtle bugs.

This pattern recurs in Exam 3 (mirror constructor verification via traversal outputs) and HW6 (preOrderInOrderBuild reconstruction); understanding how each traversal order encodes different information about tree structure will help you predict and verify traversal outputs.
